newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian papers speculate on embattled PM's future.
newsitem.headline: Russian papers speculate on embattled PM's future.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's call for a government shake-up has given a fresh turn to Russia's political rumour-mill with two newspapers predicting the changes may even engulf Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

Quoting a "well-informed source from the prime minister's own circle", the liberal daily Izvestia said on Wednesday that Chernomyrdin, longtime symbol of Russian political stability for the outside world, had outlived his usefulness.
"The political decision on Chernomyrdin's dismissal has already been taken," it said in its main front-page article.
The respected weekly Moskovskiye Novosti also said Yeltsin was planning to drop his loyal understudy, who has headed the Russian government for more than four years.

Citing a senior member of the State Duma lower house of parliament, the paper said Chernomyrdin, 58, would be sacked for two reasons -- Russia's continuing economic slump and what it called his closeness to Yeltsin's communist and nationalist foes.
Officials dismissed the reports, noting that the Kremlin had said earlier this week that the premier's place was secure.
"The papers are always writing things and we cannot react to every article," a government press spokeswoman told Reuters.

But the articles reflected increased jitters in Russian political circles ahead of Yeltsin's annual address to parliament on March 6 which is expected to focus on pressing economic and social problems like wage and pension arrears.
Non-payment of wages and pensions is a major reason for the government's unpopularity. Locked in a web of debt, many firms say they cannot pay their workers.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is bankrolling reforms with a $10 billion three-year loan, but on Tuesday it said it was not ready to hand over more cash. The IMF is worried by low tax revenues and delays in restructuring Soviet-era factories.
On Monday Yeltsin told Chernomyrdin in televised remarks that some ministers should be dropped to help defuse rising social tensions and improve the government's efficiency.

Yeltsin, 66, is keen to show he is firmly back in charge after recovering first from November's heart surgery and then from pneumonia and needs to make some sacrifices to put his stamp firmly back on Russian politics, commentators said.

If the stout, balding Chernomyrdin were dismissed, Izvestia said his most likely successor was either Yegor Stroyev, the equally stolid chairman of the Federation Council, or more controversially, Yeltsin's chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais.
Chubais, a youthful liberal who spearheaded Russia's huge privatisation campaign, is a hate figure for the communist and nationalist opposition who dominate the Duma.
They say he amassed huge personal power during Yeltsin's long sickness and absence from the Kremlin and also accuse him of financial irregularities. Chubais denies the charges.
Izvestia cited recent criticism by prominent liberals like Yegor Gaidar, Chernomyrdin's successor who launched radical market reforms in 1992, calling for the government's removal.
Gaidar said Chernomyrdin, a grey bureaucrat, was pushing the country into crisis with inconsistent policies.

Izvestia said Gaidar himself might join the economic team of a new cabinet. There has been no indication, however, that Yeltsin was ready to summon back his old-time ally who has no strong political base or public backing.

The pro-reform Nezavisimaya Gazeta said on Wednesday that Chernomyrdin, whose main task in government has been balancing liberal and conservative forces, was too cautious and seemed incapable of taking the radical measures that Russia needs.
But it added, drawing an image from chess: "The president is hardly likely to sacrifice his queen in the foreseeable future."
"In Russia, just as there is no alternative to the president, so there is also no alternative to the prime minister," the paper added.
